definition: Cloud deployment model in which a provider hosts many unrelated tenants on shared infrastructure that any customer can subscribe to over the internet.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 10: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models

definition: Cloud deployment model dedicated to a single organization, on its own or reserved hardware, giving the most control over data and security.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 10: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models

definition: Cloud deployment model that combines on-premises or dedicated infrastructure with provider-hosted services, so workloads and data can move between the two.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 10: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models

definition: Cloud deployment model shared by several organizations with common needs, such as firms in one industry, which split the cost of a dedicated infrastructure.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 10: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models

definition: Strategy of using services from two or more different cloud providers at once, which avoids depending on one vendor and survives an outage at any single provider.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Cloud model in which developers upload code as functions and the provider runs, scales, and patches all underlying machines, while the customer still secures its code and data.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 10: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models

definition: Practice of defining servers, networks, and other resources in machine-readable files, such as YAML or JSON, so they deploy the same way every time and stay under version control.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 10: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models

definition: Chart showing which security duties belong to the cloud provider and which to the customer for each service type, such as IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 10: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models; SY0-801 objective 3.1

definition: Hosting model in which an organization owns and runs its servers in its own buildings, giving it full control of security but also full responsibility for hardware, power, and staff.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 10: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models

definition: Network physically isolated from the internet and every other network, with no wired or wireless links, so data moves in or out only on removable media.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 10: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models

definition: Design that splits an application into small, independent services, each with one business function, that talk through APIs and can be deployed, scaled, and fail separately.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 10: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models

definition: Dividing a network into separate parts with software controls, such as VLANs, subnets, and firewall rules, while devices may still share the same switches and cables.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 10: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models

definition: Separating networks with their own dedicated switches, cabling, and hardware, so traffic in one part cannot reach another through shared equipment.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 10: Comparing and Contrasting Security Implications of Different Architecture Models; SY0-801 objective 3.1

definition: Ability of a system to keep working through faults, attacks, or disasters and to return to normal quickly, achieved with redundancy and recovery planning.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 10: Comparing and Contrasting Security Implications of Different Architecture Models

definition: How easy a system is for people to use; security controls that make work hard push users toward workarounds that weaken protection.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 10: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models; SY0-801 objective 3.1

definition: How quickly and simply a system can be brought back to working order after a failure or attack, for example from backups, snapshots, or code templates.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 10: Comparing and Contrasting Security Implications of Different Architecture Models

definition: Ability of a system to grow or shrink its capacity to handle more or less work, by adding resources to a node or by adding more nodes.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 10: Comparing and Contrasting Security Implications of Different Architecture Models

definition: The processing capacity, such as CPU cores and memory, that a design needs; security functions like encryption and traffic inspection add to this demand.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 10: Comparing and Contrasting Security Implications of Different Architecture Models

definition: Electricity a design needs for its servers, cooling, and network gear, including backup supply, which can limit where and how systems are deployed.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 10: Comparing and Contrasting Security Implications of Different Architecture Models; SY0-801 objective 3.1

definition: Software whose code anyone may read and change; a large community can find and fix its flaws, but support and patch timing are not guaranteed.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 10: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models; SY0-801 objective 3.1

definition: Software owned by a vendor that keeps its code secret; the vendor supplies support and patches, but customers cannot audit the code and may be locked in.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 10: Compare and contrast security implications of different architecture models; SY0-801 objective 3.1

definition: Deciding where each security appliance, such as a firewall, IDS sensor, or jump server, sits in the network so it can see and protect the right traffic.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 11: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

definition: Network area grouped by trust level, such as the internal LAN, the boundary network, or the internet, with its own access rules enforced where traffic crosses it.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 11: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

definition: Boundary network between the internet and the internal LAN, guarded by firewalls, that holds public-facing servers such as web and mail servers.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 11: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

definition: All the points where an attacker could try to get in or pull data out, such as open ports, running services, accounts, endpoints, and third-party links.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 11: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

definition: Layering controls from different vendors or of different types, such as two firewall brands, so a single flaw or exploit cannot defeat every layer.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: Failure mode in which a security device that stops working blocks all traffic or access, keeping protection at the cost of availability.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 11: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: Failure mode in which a security device that stops working lets all traffic or access through, keeping service up but leaving the network unprotected.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 11: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: Network design that places policy decision and enforcement points in front of every resource, so each request is checked for identity, device health, and context before access.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 11: Applying Security Principles to Secure Enterprise Infrastructure; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: An endpoint's current security condition, such as patch level, running antivirus, and enabled disk encryption, checked as a condition for granting access.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 11: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: Up-to-date record of every endpoint allowed to reach company resources, so unknown or unmanaged devices can be spotted and denied.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 11: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: Granting a verified user entry to one specific program or web app after checking identity and context, instead of opening the whole network to that user.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 11: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: Encrypted connection across an untrusted network, such as the internet, that lets a remote user or branch office reach an internal network as if attached locally.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 11: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

definition: Ability to reach and use a computer or network from another location, for example through SSH, RDP, or a VPN client, which must be secured and logged.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 11: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

definition: Wrapping one protocol's packets inside another, usually encrypted, protocol so they cross an untrusted network privately, as IPsec and TLS do for VPNs.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 11: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

definition: Suite of protocols that authenticates and encrypts IP packets with AH and ESP headers, widely used for site-to-site and remote VPN connections.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 11: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

definition: Cloud architecture that merges wide-area networking such as SD-WAN with cloud-delivered security services under a Zero Trust model, for users in any location.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 11: Given a scenario, apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

definition: Encrypted method of copying documents between hosts inside an SSH session on port 22, protecting both the login and the content.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 18: Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: Communication in which only the sender's and recipient's devices hold the keys, so the servers that relay the messages cannot read their content.
source: Mobile Communications Best Practice Guidance – CISA; End-to-end encryption – Wikipedia; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: Administering servers and network devices through a separate, dedicated channel, such as a management network or console port, that keeps working when the production network is down.
source: Essential Guide to Out-of-Band Management – Advantech; Out-of-band management – Wikipedia; Performing Out-of-Band Network Management – NSA; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: Cloud-delivered bundle of security services, chiefly a secure web gateway, a cloud access security broker, and Zero Trust network access, that protects users wherever they connect.
source: What Is Security Service Edge (SSE)? – Palo Alto Networks Cyberpedia; What is Global Secure Access? – Microsoft Learn; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: Active Directory account for running services on one or more servers, whose long password the domain controllers generate and rotate automatically so no administrator handles it.
source: Microsoft Learn – Group Managed Service Accounts overview; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: User account with only the rights needed for daily work, kept separate from any administrator account so that malware or mistakes during normal use do limited damage.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 23: Summarizing Elements of Effective Security Governance; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: Gradual build-up of access rights as a user changes jobs and keeps old permissions, leaving far more access than the current role needs.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 20: Understanding the Importance of Automation and Orchestration Related to Secure Operations; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: Administering people's accounts across their life cycle: creating them, assigning and changing rights, and disabling them promptly when people leave.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 20: Understanding the Importance of Automation and Orchestration Related to Secure Operations; SY0-801 objective 3.2

definition: Data organized in a fixed, predefined format such as the rows and columns of a database table, which makes it easy to search, classify, and protect field by field.
source: IBM Think – Structured vs. unstructured data: What's the difference?; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Data with no predefined format, such as emails, documents, images, audio, and video, which is harder to search and classify and often hides sensitive content.
source: IBM Think – Structured vs. unstructured data: What's the difference?; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Data stored on a drive, database, file share, or backup medium and not currently moving or being processed, protected mainly with disk, file, or database encryption.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Data moving across a network or communication channel, such as a web purchase, protected mainly with protocols like TLS, HTTPS, and IPsec.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Data loaded into memory and being processed by an application or CPU, where it is usually unencrypted and must be protected by measures such as secure enclaves.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Process of sorting information into labeled levels by sensitivity and the harm its exposure would cause, which then decides how it is stored, accessed, and destroyed.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 12: Comparing and Contrasting Concepts and Strategies to Protect Data

definition: Highest government level, for information whose unauthorized release could cause exceptionally grave damage to national security.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Government level just below the highest, for information whose unauthorized release could cause serious damage to national security.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Label for information whose disclosure would cause damage; the lowest government level that is still classified, and in business often used for trade secrets and source code.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Commercial label for the most tightly controlled information, which only named people may access and whose use legal or regulatory rules also limit.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 12: Comparing and Contrasting Concepts and Strategies to Protect Data

definition: Label for information such as PII or internal financial details whose exposure could harm people or the organization, so it needs more protection than open information.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Label for information the organization cannot operate without, such as encryption keys or core databases, whose loss or corruption would halt the business.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 12: Comparing and Contrasting Concepts and Strategies to Protect Data

definition: Label for information approved for anyone to see, such as press releases and brochures, whose release causes no harm.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Label for personal or internal information, such as salaries and medical records, that is not meant for outsiders and whose exposure would harm the people it describes.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 12: Comparing and Contrasting Concepts and Strategies to Protect Data

definition: Applying rules that remove or block sensitive values, such as card numbers, from information before it is displayed, sent, or shared, as content filters and DLP tools do.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 18: Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Hiding information by rearranging the order of its characters or fields by a set rule, so the original pieces remain but no longer read in their true order.
source: Understanding and Selecting Data Masking: Defining Data Masking – Securosis; Transposition cipher – Wikipedia; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Removing or altering details that link records to specific people, such as names and ID numbers, so a data set can be used without revealing who it describes.
source: NIST CSRC Glossary – de-identification; NIST SP 800-188, De-Identifying Government Data Sets; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Limiting access to information so that only users or devices located in approved countries or regions can reach it, often to satisfy local regulations.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Limiting who can read, change, or delete information by assigning rights according to each user's role, so only authorized staff can handle it.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Senior person accountable for a data set, who decides its classification and who may access it, and answers for its protection.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 23: Summarize elements of effective security governance; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Role, usually in IT, that carries out the technical safeguarding of information day to day: storing it securely, encrypting it, backing it up, and applying retention rules.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 23: Summarize elements of effective security governance; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Role that keeps information accurate and consistent, fixes errors, maintains metadata, and labels it by sensitivity so it is understood and handled correctly.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 23: Summarize elements of effective security governance; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Organization or person that decides why and how personal information is collected and used, and is legally responsible for following privacy laws such as GDPR.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 23: Summarize elements of effective security governance; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Organization that handles personal information on behalf of the party that decided its purpose, following that party's written instructions and keeping records of its work.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 23: Summarize elements of effective security governance

definition: Third party that a company already handling personal information for a client hires to do part of that work; it needs the client's approval and the same contract terms.
source: GDPR Article 28 (Processor); UK ICO – Controllers and processors; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Attaching a visible tag or metadata to files, documents, and media that shows their sensitivity level, so people and tools such as DLP handle them correctly.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 12: Comparing and Contrasting Concepts and Strategies to Protect Data; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Using GPS or network location to draw a virtual boundary, so a device or app changes features, data access, or alerts as it enters or leaves the area.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 14: Applying Common Security Techniques to Computing Resources; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Working out the real-world location of a user or device from GPS, IP address, or Wi-Fi data, to check that a login or request comes from an expected place.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Principle that information is subject to the laws of the country where it is collected or stored, which limits where an organization or cloud provider may move or keep it.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Sequence of stages that information passes through from the moment it is made or collected until it is securely destroyed, with controls applied at each stage.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 23: Summarize elements of effective security governance; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Stage in which information is first generated or collected, the right moment to classify and label it and to assign who is accountable for it.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 23: Summarize elements of effective security governance; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Stage in which stored information is organized, kept accurate, and protected with access controls and backups during its working life.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 23: Summarize elements of effective security governance; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Stage in which information is shared with users, partners, or other systems, which calls for encryption in transit and checks that each recipient is authorized.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 23: Summarize elements of effective security governance; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Keeping information only for the period that policy, law, or contract sets before it may be destroyed; the same rule sets how long backup copies are kept.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 23: Summarize elements of effective security governance; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Final stage, in which information that is no longer needed is destroyed so it cannot be recovered, for example by wiping, degaussing, or shredding media.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 23: Summarize elements of effective security governance; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Information whose collection, storage, and sharing are governed by specific laws or industry rules, such as medical records under HIPAA or card data under PCI DSS.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 12: Comparing and Contrasting Concepts and Strategies to Protect Data

definition: Any information that can identify a specific individual on its own or combined with other details, such as a name, ID number, email address, or biometric record.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Medical details linked to a specific person, such as diagnoses, treatments, test results, and insurance records, safeguarded in the United States by HIPAA.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Information about payments, bank accounts, card numbers, transactions, and an organization's accounts, protected by rules such as PCI DSS, GLBA, and SOX.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Personal information about people under the legal age of consent, which laws such as the US COPPA protect by requiring a parent's verifiable permission before collecting it.
source: US FTC – Complying with COPPA: Frequently Asked Questions; Wikipedia – Children's Online Privacy Protection Act; SY0-801 objective 3.3

definition: Creations of the mind, such as inventions, designs, source code, and written works, protected by patents, copyrights, and trademarks.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Information about court cases, contracts, and litigation, often protected by attorney-client privilege and needing strict handling and retention.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 12: Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

definition: Confidential business know-how, such as a formula or algorithm, that gives a competitive edge and is protected by NDAs and access limits rather than registration.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 12: Comparing and Contrasting Concepts and Strategies to Protect Data

definition: Fully equipped standby facility with data replicated in near real time, ready to take over operations within minutes; the fastest and most expensive recovery option.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Standby facility with hardware and connectivity in place but data that is only periodically updated, so it needs hours or days of work before taking over.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Standby facility that provides only space, power, and cooling, with no ready equipment or data, so recovery takes the longest but costs the least.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Placing data centers and backups far apart in different regions, so one regional disaster such as a flood or long power outage cannot take out all of them.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Spreading incoming requests across several servers, sending each to a healthy, lightly used one, so no server is overloaded and one failure does not stop the service.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Grouping two or more servers that share storage and watch each other through a heartbeat, so a standby node takes over at once if the active one fails.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Cloud feature that automatically adds or removes instances as measured demand rises and falls, keeping performance steady without paying for unused capacity.
source: AWS – Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling User Guide and FAQs; SY0-801 objective 3.4

definition: Design goal of keeping a service running with almost no downtime, often stated as a percentage such as 99.999 percent, through redundant parts with no single point of failure.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Running workloads on a mix of operating systems, hardware types, or virtualization platforms, so a flaw or failure in one technology does not stop every system.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Buying critical products or services from more than one supplier, so one supplier's outage, flaw, or business failure does not leave the organization without a working option.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 13: Understanding the Importance of Resilience and Recovery in Security Architecture; SY0-801 objective 3.4

definition: Battery-backed device that supplies power instantly when mains power fails, long enough to ride out short outages, shut systems down cleanly, or start a generator.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Second power unit in a server or network device, often hot-swappable, that keeps the device running on its own if the first unit fails.
source: Oracle Server X9-2 Service Manual – Servicing Power Supplies; Install a hot-swap power supply unit – Lenovo ThinkSystem SR645 Docs; SY0-801 objective 3.4

definition: Fuel-driven machine that produces electricity for hours or days during a long outage, usually started while battery units bridge the first minutes.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Device that shields connected equipment from sudden voltage spikes, such as those caused by lightning, by diverting the excess energy away.
source: NIST CSRC Glossary – Surge Protector (NISTIR 7621 Rev. 1); SY0-801 objective 3.4

definition: Rack-mounted strip that feeds power to the equipment in a rack; managed models let staff monitor the load and switch outlets remotely.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Copy of all selected data every time the job runs; the slowest and largest kind, but a restore needs only that one set.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Copy of only the data changed since the last backup of any kind; fast and small, but a restore needs the last full set plus every later one in order.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Copy of all data changed since the last full backup; it grows each day, but a restore needs only the full set and the latest one of these.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Point-in-time image of a virtual machine or storage volume, including its state, that lets administrators roll back quickly to that moment.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Continuously copying data to another system or site in near real time, so an up-to-date duplicate is ready if the primary fails.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Recording every change to files or a database, with time and details, in a log that can be replayed to restore data to a precise point.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Copy of data locked against change or deletion, even by administrators, until its retention period ends, so ransomware cannot encrypt or erase it.
source: IBM Think – What are immutable backups?; Cohesity glossary – Immutable backup; SY0-801 objective 3.4

definition: Regularly recovering data from saved copies onto a test system to prove the copies are complete, readable, and can be brought back within the target time.
source: SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems – NIST CSRC; #StopRansomware Guide – CISA; SY0-801 objective 3.4

definition: Decision about which systems, data, and settings a backup job includes, such as whole servers, single databases, or chosen folders.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 13: Understanding the Importance of Resilience and Recovery in Security Architecture; SY0-801 objective 3.4

definition: Process for restoring IT systems, data, and facilities after a major disruption, setting out restoration steps, priorities, and alternate locations.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture; SY0-801 objective 3.4

definition: Effort that keeps an organization's essential functions running during and after a disruption, covering people, processes, and suppliers, not only IT systems.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture; SY0-801 objective 3.4

definition: Forecasting the people, technology, and infrastructure needed to meet future demand, so systems and teams are not overwhelmed during growth or a crisis.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Switching operations from a failed primary system to a standby one; trying it on purpose proves the standby actually takes over without losing data.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 13: Explain the importance of resilience and recovery in security architecture

definition: Check that runs the same workloads on the primary and the recovery systems at the same time and compares their results, without interrupting production.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Cert Guide (Heuermann), Pearson – Chapter 13: Understanding the Importance of Resilience and Recovery in Security Architecture

definition: Target for how long a system or process may stay down after a disruption before the outage causes unacceptable harm; restoration must finish within it.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 24: Explain elements of the risk management process; SY0-801 objective 3.4

definition: Maximum amount of data, measured as time before an outage, that the organization can afford to lose; it sets how often backups must run.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 24: Explain elements of the risk management process; SY0-801 objective 3.4

definition: Average duration needed to fix a failed component or system and return it to service.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 24: Explain elements of the risk management process; SY0-801 objective 3.4

definition: Average period of normal operation from one breakdown of a repairable system to the next, used to predict its reliability.
source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Certification Guide, 3rd ed. (Neil), Packt – Chapter 24: Explain elements of the risk management process; SY0-801 objective 3.4
